How Product Managers Alienate Engineers

Being mysterious, explaining how, hoarding credit, throwing blame and hurrying-up-then-waiting are not manners problems. They are informational acts with computable consequences, and the field does not agree about what to do with them.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On 14 April 2026, Rohan Deshmukh sat in a glass room on the fourth floor of Vismay's office in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, looking at a resignation and two internal transfer requests. Vismay is a consumer running and cycling app: 4.1 million monthly actives, 218,000 paying subscribers at ₹399 a quarter, a Series C round being assembled on the strength of a “Clubs” relaunch that had to demo on 8 June. Rohan was the group PM for the social surface. The two transfer requests were from the only two Android engineers who understood the app's background-location code, and both had been filed within five days of each other. Neither engineer had complained about anything. The engineering director, Preeti Mohan, told Rohan that in her experience this was the normal sequence: the complaints stop first, and the transfers follow about nine weeks later.

On 21 April, 840 kilometres north-west, Sunita Kalburgi was in a very different room. Hiranmay Systems, in Hinjawadi, Pune, sells plant-maintenance software to heavy industry — 38 enterprise customers, ₹210 crore of annual recurring revenue, on-premise deployments at 140 plant sites across India and the Gulf. On 12 March, an upgrade to release 9.4 at a cement major's Chandrapur plant had failed; maintenance scheduling was offline for 31 hours; the customer's CIO had escalated twice; a ₹31 crore renewal was under review. In the post-incident review, it emerged that a senior engineer, Vinod Salunke, had flagged the underlying Modbus TCP driver timeout in a code-review comment on 2 February and had not escalated it further. Asked why, he said, in front of eleven people, “The last time I raised something late in a cycle it appeared in the monthly update as an engineering delay, with my initials next to it.” The engineering organisation now wanted a written working agreement with product. Sunita, Director of Product, had to decide whether that was a governance improvement or a vote of no confidence in her function.

2. The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree about it

Define alienation precisely. It is the progressive withdrawal of two goods that an engineer supplies voluntarily and that no employment contract can compel: discretionary effort, meaning the care taken beyond the literal requirements of a ticket, and discretionary disclosure, meaning the volunteering of bad news before anyone has asked for it. The second is the more valuable and the first to go. Vinod Salunke did his job on 2 February — he left a code-review comment. What he withheld was the escalation, and the escalation is the part that was worth ₹42 lakh in service credits.

The intellectual lineage runs longer than product management. Karl Marx's 1844 manuscripts introduced alienated labour as the separation of the worker from purpose and product. Frederick Herzberg's motivation-hygiene research in 1959 established the asymmetry that still confuses managers: the factors whose presence produces satisfaction are not the factors whose absence produces misery, so fixing pay does not fix meaning. Fred Brooks, writing in The Mythical Man-Month in 1975, supplied the craft argument — that conceptual integrity is authored, that engineers are not interchangeable capacity, and that treating them as such is both inefficient and insulting. Edward Deci and Richard Ryan's self-determination theory, formalised in 1985, named the three needs whose satisfaction sustains intrinsic motivation: autonomy, competence and relatedness. Tom DeMarco and Timothy Lister brought all of this into software management with Peopleware in 1987. Kent Beck made it procedural in Extreme Programming in 1999, with the rule that the customer decides what and the developers decide how, codified in a mutual bill of rights.

Two later strands matter because they made the topic measurable. Amy Edmondson's 1999 work on psychological safety, later popularised by Google's Project Aristotle in 2015, defined the variable as the shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking, and found it predicted team performance better than composition did. And Ron Westrum's 1993 typology of organisational information climates — pathological, bureaucratic, generative — was picked up by the DORA research programme and published in Accelerate (Forsgren, Humble and Kim, 2018), which found the Westrum measure correlated with software delivery performance across thousands of organisations. Westrum's operational definition is the one to hold on to: in a pathological climate, messengers are shot, responsibility is shirked and failure leads to scapegoating. Two of the five behaviours in this topic — throwing blame and being mysterious — are precisely the local, PM-level version of a pathological climate.

That history produces genuine disagreement rather than a consensus. Five positions are worth being able to state in their strongest form, because a practitioner who cannot tell them apart will apply the wrong remedy.

3. Mechanics in depth: why one bad Monday costs four months

The mechanism that makes this topic worth studying rather than merely believing is the asymmetry between damage and repair. It is not sentiment. It is inference, and it can be computed.

Treat an engineer as holding a belief about a single proposition: my PM behaves well when under pressure. Suppose Vinod Salunke's prior, in December, was 0.80 — a normal degree of professional confidence. In January he observes one blame event: his initials next to a slipped date in a monthly update. What is the likelihood of that observation? If the PM really is reliable under pressure, such an event is rare: call it 0.05. If the PM is not, it is common: call it 0.60. Bayes then gives a posterior of 0.80 × 0.05 divided by (0.80 × 0.05 + 0.20 × 0.60), which is 0.04 / 0.16, which is 0.25. One observation moved an eighty-per-cent belief to a twenty-five-per-cent belief, and it did so correctly.

Recovery runs on the same arithmetic, and this is where most repair plans fail. A good observation — the PM handling a pressured moment well — has likelihood 0.95 under the reliable hypothesis and 0.40 under the unreliable one, a likelihood ratio of 2.375. Starting from posterior odds of 0.25/0.75 = 0.333, three such observations are needed to climb back above 0.80. The critical restriction is that only pressured observations carry that ratio. Behaving well on an ordinary Tuesday has a likelihood ratio of roughly 1.0, because reliable and unreliable PMs are indistinguishable when nothing is at stake. If genuine pressure events occur roughly every six weeks, restoration takes about eighteen weeks.

Three second-order effects follow, and expert practitioners watch for all three because each one disguises the original cause.

Estimate inflation. An engineer who cannot control the how will buy control back through the only lever left, which is the when. At Vismay, Preeti Mohan's data showed the median estimate-to-actual ratio on the social squad moving from 1.08 to 1.62 over two quarters. The more diagnostic number was the variance: the spread of that ratio collapsed from a range of 0.6–1.9 to 1.45–1.80. Honest estimates vary because tasks vary. Padded estimates cluster, because padding is a policy rather than a judgement. The PM then observes inflated estimates, concludes that engineering is sandbagging, applies pressure, and closes the loop.

Information re-routing. Once a PM is an unsafe destination for bad news, the news does not stop; it finds another path, usually to the engineering manager or the designer. The PM discovers problems later and from third parties, experiences this as being cut out, and responds by demanding more status reporting, which the squad reads as surveillance. This is the loop that turns a recoverable situation into a structural one, and its tell is a PM who starts asking for daily written updates.

Adverse selection in attrition. The engineers with the most external options leave first, which means the average capability of the remaining team falls. The PM's low opinion of the team then becomes accurate, which makes the diagnosis harder rather than easier. Rohan's two Android engineers were, by Preeti's reckoning, the two most employable people on the squad.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Five structural situations break the simple model, and in each one the honest account of what large organisations do differs from what they say.

The platform seam: many PMs, no relationship

Hiranmay's data-ingestion platform team of nine engineers serves six product PMs. No single PM owns the relationship, so no single PM is responsible for the climate. The arithmetic is brutal: if each PM is individually reliable 85 per cent of the time, the probability that a platform engineer experiences at least one alienating interaction in a given fortnight is 1 − 0.855 = 0.556. Five good PMs produce a bad environment. Mature organisations handle this not by exhorting PMs to be better but by appointing a single platform PM who intermediates — converting five relationships into one — and they rarely describe it that way, because the stated reason is usually roadmap coherence.

Two-sided products: the “why” is contested

In a marketplace, the PM's explanation of purpose is not a neutral good, because the two sides of the market are in partial conflict. Engineers who have spent two years on supply-side tooling hear a demand-side strategy as a statement that their work no longer matters. The competent move is not a better explanation but an explicit statement of the trade-off and its expiry: which side is being favoured, by how much, for how long, and what would change it.

Regulated environments: blamelessness has a legal ceiling

Hiranmay's post-incident report on the Chandrapur outage would be read by the customer's audit function. A genuinely blameless internal narrative and a contractually defensible external one are not the same document, and pretending otherwise is naive. What mature organisations actually do is maintain two artefacts — an internal learning review with no names attached to causes, and an external report written by legal and commercial functions — and, crucially, tell the engineers that both exist. The alienating version is the one where engineers discover the second document by accident.

Hardware-plus-software: hurry-up-then-wait is built into the calendar

Where a physical milestone exists — a tooling freeze, a certification submission — the software team is genuinely rushed to a date and then genuinely waits eleven weeks for moulds or approvals. The behaviour is structural, not a PM failure, and treating it as one is unhelpful. The distinction that matters is whether the wait was forecast and named in advance. A predicted eleven-week wait is a plan; an unexplained eleven-week wait is the fifth behaviour in this topic.

AI-native products: the outcome/mechanism boundary genuinely blurs

When behaviour is produced by a model rather than by code, the PM cannot fully specify the outcome, because the outcome is empirical. Prompts, evaluation sets and model selection sit ambiguously between the two spaces. Two new alienation patterns have emerged. The first is the PM who writes evaluation criteria without invitation and is experienced as taking over the specification. The second, more corrosive, is the PM who builds a working demonstration with a model over a weekend and presents it to leadership as nearly finished — a new and extremely effective form of hurry-up-then-wait, because it compresses the perceived remaining work to near zero in the minds of everyone except the people who have to productionise it. Rohan had done exactly this in February with a Clubs prototype, and Preeti believed it was the proximate cause of one of the two transfer requests.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Silence is the signal; complaint is health

A squad that argues about scope is spending energy on an outcome it believes it can influence. The expert's tell is not a heated planning session but a placid one — an estimate accepted without challenge, a ticket closed exactly as written, a design review with no questions. The obvious reading of a quiet team is alignment. The correct reading is usually that the arguing has moved somewhere the PM cannot hear it.

Estimate variance is a better readout than estimate level

Everyone watches whether estimates are going up. The expert watches whether they are converging. Genuine estimates disperse because tasks differ in difficulty; defensive estimates cluster because the padding is applied as a uniform policy. A squad whose estimate-to-actual ratios all fall between 1.45 and 1.80 is not estimating; it is negotiating.

The PM is frequently a transmitter rather than a source

Before concluding that a PM has caused alienation, the expert asks what pressure that PM is absorbing and from whom. A PM who is being asked by a founder for a date every second day will manufacture urgency without any intent to manipulate. The tell is a correlation: check whether the PM's urgency events cluster within forty-eight hours of leadership reviews. If they do, the remedy is upstream, and coaching the PM will produce compliance without change.

Credit is allocated by artefact, not by intention

Almost no PM decides to take credit. Credit accrues to whoever narrates, and PMs narrate for a living. The expert's diagnostic is mechanical and takes ninety seconds: open the last ten launch notes and count the named engineers. The usual answer is zero, and the usual cause is a template.

Blame is read from grammar

“Engineering slipped” feels impersonal to the writer and personal to the reader, because the passive construction is understood as a refusal to co-own a date the PM also agreed to. Experts scan status updates for agentless constructions the way an editor scans for cliché. The replacement is not self-blame but the first-person plural with a specific cause attached: we mis-scoped the tenant authentication work, and here is the new date and why we believe it.

Alienation and burnout look identical and require opposite treatments

Both present as low output, low disclosure and flat affect. Burnout is depletion and is treated by reducing load. Alienation is disengagement and is treated by increasing autonomy and context. The treatments are not merely different; each is harmful in the other case. Giving an alienated engineer two weeks off returns them to the same conditions with a fortnight's less momentum; giving a burnt-out engineer more ownership adds weight to someone already at the limit. The separating question is not how the person feels but what they do with slack: an alienated engineer given a free afternoon builds something of their own, and a burnt-out one sleeps.

Urgency is an instrument, and instruments can be recalibrated

The normative model says that a squad should surge whenever the expected cost of missing a genuine emergency exceeds the cost of surging. At Vismay those numbers were roughly 40 engineer-days against 6, implying that a squad should surge even when only 15 per cent of urgency calls are genuine. Observed behaviour does not follow the model: surge intensity tracked credibility almost linearly, falling from 94 per cent of requested effort at high credibility to about 55 per cent at low. The gap between the normative and the observed is the finding. People are not running an expected-value calculation; they are running a reciprocity calculation, and the reciprocity calculation punishes the PM at precisely the moment the expected-value calculation says it should not.

Trust balances are held by individuals and are inherited

A new PM inherits the deficit of the last one and experiences the resulting scepticism as unfair, which it is, and as irrational, which it is not. The expert's move on joining an area is to ask three archaeological questions: what did the previous PM promise that did not happen; who here was overruled on a technical decision and by whom; and when did someone last raise a risk early and what happened to them.

The most valuable people leave most quietly

Loud dissatisfaction is a form of investment; people argue about things they expect to stay for. The person to worry about is the one who used to argue and has stopped. At Vismay, neither of the two Android engineers had raised a concern in the preceding quarter, and Preeti regarded that fact, not the transfer requests, as the actual data point.

Repair must be over-invested at the start and under-celebrated throughout

Because only pressured observations move the posterior, a repair plan produces no measurable signal for one to two quarters. Practitioners abandon repairs at about week six, when the survey has not moved, and conclude the diagnosis was wrong. The expert budgets for the flat section in advance and tells their own manager that the metric will not move until the third pressured episode, which converts an apparent failure into an expected one.

7. How this varies by product type and company stage

Some claimed differences here are real and some are folklore. The folklore worth killing first: the idea that engineers in consumer companies care more about purpose than engineers in enterprise companies. They do not. What differs is the channel. A consumer engineer can discover purpose by using the product; an enterprise engineer at Hiranmay will never stand in a cement plant at 3 a.m. and therefore depends entirely on the PM for it. Withholding context in B2B is not stinginess; it is the abuse of a monopoly.

8. Three worked examples, including one repair that failed

Example one: Vismay's code-red sprint, 16–27 February 2026

Rohan declared the Clubs relaunch urgent on 16 February. The squad of nine had 81 engineer-days of sprint capacity; 52 went to Clubs. Two items were displaced: the Android background-location migration, 12 engineer-days, and payment-retry hardening, 7. Eight engineer-days of weekend work were volunteered. The Clubs work finished on 27 February and shipped on 10 April, because the design iteration was not complete — six weeks of waiting after two weeks of hurrying. Meanwhile the displaced location migration missed a store policy deadline of 31 March; the app update was rejected on 2 April; the scramble took 16 engineer-days, the release train stopped for four days, and 2,760 subscription renewals lapsed at ₹399 each. At Vismay's loaded rate of ₹26,000 per engineer-day, that is 16 × ₹26,000 = ₹4.16 lakh, plus ₹11.01 lakh of lapsed renewals, or ₹15.17 lakh — against a benefit of zero, since the feature waited six weeks anyway. Had Rohan stated on 16 February that the real gate was the 8 June board demo, the same 52 engineer-days would have spread across three sprints with 243 days of capacity, the migration would have shipped on time, and nothing would have been lost. The changed input is one sentence containing a date.

Example two: Hiranmay's withheld risk

Vinod Salunke's code-review comment of 2 February identified the Modbus TCP timeout under a specific PLC firmware revision. Fixing it before the 12 March upgrade would have taken an estimated 3 engineer-days. It was not escalated. The Chandrapur upgrade failed; maintenance scheduling was offline 31 hours; remediation consumed 9 person-weeks, or 45 engineer-days at ₹19,000 loaded, which is ₹8.55 lakh; contractual service credits came to ₹42 lakh; and a ₹31 crore renewal went under review. The ratio of the early fix to the late one is 3 to 45 on effort alone, and roughly 1 to 170 including credits. The cost was incurred in March. The cause was a sentence in a January status update.

Example three: the repair that made things worse

This is the instructive one. In 2025, Rohan's predecessor at Vismay, Ira Bhattacharya, recognised the problem and responded with ceremony: a three-day offsite in Coorg for 22 people costing ₹8.4 lakh, two facilitated candour workshops, and a redesigned launch slide with everyone's name on it. Pre-emptive disclosure rose from 38 per cent to 44 per cent within a fortnight, then fell to 29 per cent by week eight — below where it had started.

Why did the expensive attempt fail? The Bayesian account is exact. An offsite supplies a large number of observations with a likelihood ratio near 1.0 — pleasant behaviour under no pressure is equally probable from a reliable and an unreliable PM, so it is uninformative. The recovery that worked cost nothing and consisted of a single mechanical change applied consistently through five months and three genuinely pressured episodes. The lesson is not that offsites are useless. It is that ceremonies change stated norms while only pressured episodes change beliefs, and an unmatched pair of the two is worse than neither.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Three disputes in this area are live, and none of them is resolved by a synthesis that anyone actually holds.

Is the cause individual or systemic?

The systems position, in its strongest form, rests on Deming's claim that the overwhelming majority of variation in outcomes is attributable to the system rather than to the people in it, and on the DORA finding that Westrum's organisational climate measure predicts delivery performance at the organisational level. On this view, naming a PM as the cause of an alienated squad is itself an instance of the pathological behaviour under study. The individualist position rests on within-organisation counterfactuals: two squads on the same codebase, the same cadence and the same leadership, differing only in PM, score 2.9 and 4.1. That is a controlled comparison and it is hard to argue away. What would have to be true for the systems view to be wrong is that PM-to-PM variation within a single organisation exceeds organisation-to-organisation variation; what would have to be true for the individualist view to be wrong is that the observed PM differences are downstream of differences in what each PM is asked to absorb from above. Both are testable and neither is usually tested. The platform-seam case in Figure 3 is the cleanest evidence that the systems view is sometimes simply correct.

Is accountability compatible with blamelessness?

The sceptics' case is stronger than its usual caricature. An organisation that cannot state that a team missed a commitment has no error-correction mechanism, and the rhetoric of psychological safety is, in practice, sometimes used to make commitments unenforceable. Their evidence is that high-performing organisations do impose consequences, and that teams with no consequences drift. The blameless side's evidence is the aviation and healthcare literature on incident reporting, where removing punishment for reporting raises reported error rates and lowers actual harm. The reconciliation most people gesture at — blame decisions, not people — is harder than it sounds, because decisions have authors and everyone in the room knows who they are. What would have to be true for the sceptics to be wrong is that disclosure rates, rather than effort, are the binding constraint on delivery quality; what would have to be true for the blameless side to be wrong is that teams reliably self-correct without external consequence. In Hiranmay's case the sceptics look wrong, because the binding constraint was plainly disclosure. In a team that is genuinely under-performing, they may look right.

Does individual credit help or harm?

The recognition argument is that unattributed work is demotivating and that naming people is free. The counter-argument, which has real support in the literature on forced ranking and individual incentives, is that individual attribution inside a calibrated promotion system converts collaborators into competitors, and that the most collaborative engineering cultures deliberately attribute at the level of the pair or the small group. The disagreement is genuinely unsettled and appears to depend on how promotion works in the specific organisation, which is why Vismay and Hiranmay landed on different answers to the same question in Exhibit 4.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic can recite the five behaviours and will avoid the obvious versions of each. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways. They treat pressured moments as the only moments that count, and therefore prepare for them rather than for meetings. They change artefacts rather than intentions — templates, standing agenda items, the urgency rule — because artefacts survive a bad week and intentions do not. They ask the archaeological questions when they inherit an area, and they assume the deficit is real even when they did not create it. And they are willing to say, in front of their own leadership, that a metric they are being judged on will not move for two quarters, which is the only way a repair survives the flat section of its own curve.

The negative test is equally sharp. A practitioner who responds to an alienation diagnosis with an offsite, a survey or a team charter, and who cannot name the next pressured episode on the calendar, has not internalised it.

12. What each of them decided

Rohan Deshmukh did not contest the two transfer requests, on the reasoning that an engineer who has decided to leave a team and is prevented from doing so becomes a worse problem than the vacancy. He asked Preeti Mohan for one thing instead: a thirty-minute conversation with each of the two engineers with no retention agenda and one question — what did I decide in the last six months that you would have decided differently? He then made a single mechanical change, which was that no request would carry the word urgent without a decision date and a named decider, and he told the squad he expected no visible improvement before September. He also stopped building weekend prototypes, which was the change he found hardest, because it was the one his leadership had praised him for.

Sunita Kalburgi accepted the engineering organisation's demand for a written working agreement, and reframed it before accepting: not a treaty between two parties in dispute, but a document product would draft and engineering would amend, covering what product owes engineering in context and notice, and what engineering owes product in disclosure and estimates. Her reasoning was that a demand for governance from a 260-person engineering organisation is a request for predictability rather than an accusation, and that refusing it would confirm the very unpredictability being complained about. She also changed the monthly update template so that no slip could be reported without a named cause and a first-person-plural subject — the structural fix for the structural problem that had cost ₹42 lakh.

Discussion questions. First: Vismay's counterfactual — two squads, same codebase, different PMs, 2.9 against 4.1 — is offered as evidence that the cause is individual. What alternative explanations survive that comparison, and what single piece of additional data would distinguish them?

Second: Hiranmay must produce a blameless internal review and a contractually defensible external report on the same incident. Is telling the engineers that both documents exist sufficient, and if not, what else is owed to them?

Third: Ira Bhattacharya's ₹8.4 lakh repair left the team worse off than doing nothing. Under what conditions, if any, would the same offsite have worked — and does that condition tell you anything about when to spend money on culture at all?

13. Going deeper

Madhukosh Labs: The Charter Memo

Pune, Sunday night, 11 October 2026

1. The night before

The rain had stopped over Baner around nine, and Devyani Sardesai had the flat to herself. On the dining table, in three stacks, sat the material she would have to answer for at eleven the next morning: a four-page memo signed by eleven of the twenty-three firmware and edge engineers in Pune; a board sub-committee agenda with one line item, MK-5 capital release — go / no-go; and a printout of her own Edge Behaviour Specification, seventy-one pages, requirement IDs EBS-001 to EBS-412, which she had written in March and which the memo described, without naming her, as “product defining implementation.”

Devyani, thirty-six, was Director of Product for the Vision line at Madhukosh Labs. Fourteen months earlier the line had been a ₹31 crore business with one serious customer; it was now ₹67 crore with nineteen, and carried the company's only export contract of any size. She had not expected the memo. She had, in a way she found harder to admit, half-expected the resignations that landed five days later — Ajinkya Phadke and Rukmini Das, both senior, both on the edge team, both signatories.

Three things had to settle by Monday morning and they did not settle in the same direction. The memo asked that firmware and edge scope move out of product ownership into an engineering-held “platform charter,” with Devyani reduced to a customer-requirements input. The Gulf account's foreign-material module was committed for 30 November, seven weeks away, and the forecast called the date contractual. And the board wanted a recommendation on ₹22 crore for MK-5 — a device whose justification was that the current one could not hold the models the line had promised its customers.

What she could not decide, at eleven at night, was which of those was the problem and which two were symptoms. Every reading she tried fitted about seventy per cent of the evidence.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2023

Madhukosh Labs was founded in Pune in 2014 by Nikhil Bhattacharya, an automation engineer who had spent eleven years commissioning bottling lines, and Sunanda Ghatge, who ran operations until her retirement in 2024. It builds in-line inspection systems for food and beverage manufacturing: line-scan cameras and an edge compute unit that sit above a conveyor, inspect every pack for seal integrity, fill level, label registration and foreign material, and push defect events to a console where a plant quality head sees the shift's yield by line and by SKU.

By FY26 it employed 340 people and reported ₹138 crore of revenue — ₹52 crore of hardware, ₹86 crore of subscription and services. Roughly 180 sat in Pune, where firmware and optics lived; 90 in Bengaluru, where the cloud platform and console were built; the rest across a Berlin design studio, a computer-vision group in Toronto, a customer-success desk in Singapore and a two-person sales office in New Jersey.

The decision that shaped everything Devyani now faced was made in April 2023, before she joined. To win a 4,200-unit order from a large western-India dairy cooperative — still the company's biggest single order — Madhukosh had to reach a landed price of ₹64,000 per inspection unit. It got there by freezing the MK-4 on a single system-on-chip with 2 GB of usable RAM, built under contract by a listed Indian electronics manufacturer in Tamil Nadu, and by giving the cooperative a five-year spares and firmware-compatibility guarantee. That guarantee was the load-bearing clause. Every firmware release since has had to run on every MK-4 ever shipped; and because each release triggers BIS re-testing plus the customer's own validation protocol, releases go out in four certification windows a year and not otherwise. Miss a window and the next is ninety days away.

Nobody in 2023 thought of this as a product-management constraint; it was a pricing decision. By 2026 it was the reason a model trained in Toronto could be excellent and unusable at once.

3. The industry

Indian packaged-food manufacturing has been re-equipping for a decade. FSSAI's tightening of hygiene and traceability norms, Legal Metrology enforcement on declared net quantity, and the expectations that arrive with any serious export order have pushed plant heads from sampling-based checks toward hundred-per-cent in-line inspection. Manufacturers of the scale of Amul, Britannia, Parle, Dabur, Tata Consumer Products and Hindustan Unilever have been visible in that shift, and their contract manufacturers have followed, two years behind and far more price-sensitive.

Madhukosh sells into a gap. Above it sit the global machine-vision firms — Cognex, Keyence and the vision arms of the European automation houses — whose systems are superb and cost three to five times as much per line. Below it sit Indian systems integrators and the engineering-services arms of firms such as Tata Elxsi, L&T Technology Services and Cyient, which will build a plant exactly what it asks for as a project, with no roadmap behind it. Madhukosh's claim is a product: one SKU, one console, a model library that improves without a site visit, at a price a plant manager can sign without going to the board.

Two outside forces bear on the Vision line. Manufacturers supplying European retail chains are audited against supplier standards requiring traceable detection performance for physical contaminants — not a claim of accuracy but an evidence trail from requirement to test case to field result. And the SoC family the MK-4 uses entered end-of-life notification in July 2026, with last-time-buy in March 2027.

The Gulf account — a Dubai-headquartered dairy and juice group with plants in Dubai and Al Ain, signed in October 2025 for ₹18.4 crore of subscription over three years plus ₹9.6 crore of hardware — sits at the intersection of both. A German retail chain audits its foreign-material controls, and its manufacturing excellence head, Hamdan Al Suwaidi, treats Madhukosh as a strategic supplier rather than a vendor — which is flattering and expensive at once.

4. Fourteen months

Devyani took the Vision line in August 2025. She had been at Madhukosh three years by then, after six years as an embedded-systems engineer at an automotive electronics company in Chakan — a background she mentioned often in her first months, and which Shirish Ranade, the principal firmware engineer in Pune, later said had made things worse rather than better. In October 2025 the Gulf contract was signed: seal integrity and fill level live by March 2026, foreign-material detection — the module the German audit turned on — by 30 November 2026.

In November, at Nikhil's request, Devyani signed a mutual NDA with a large Indian beverage manufacturer exploring a 900-line deployment. For eleven weeks she could not tell the Pune team what she was scoping, why she wanted throughput numbers at odd frame rates, or why two roadmap items had been deferred. She said she was “working on a large opportunity” and left it there. The deal did not close. The eleven weeks remained.

In January 2026 the board approved ₹22 crore in principle for MK-5, conditional on a FY27 pipeline review. In February the Bengaluru team began migrating to a shared monorepo and a new build toolchain — a decision made inside engineering, for good reasons, that consumed two quarters of capacity and that no exhibit since has controlled for.

In March came the specification. The German retailer's standard required traceability from requirement to test evidence, and the auditors wanted requirement IDs. Devyani wrote all 412 herself over nine days — detection thresholds, the reject-arm timing state machine, the exact error codes the PLC would see. She believed she was producing an audit artefact. The Pune team read a document telling them how to build their own firmware, delivered without a design conversation, by someone who kept mentioning that she used to write embedded code.

In May, Anousha Vaidya's group in Toronto delivered a new contaminant model at 96.1% recall on the validation set — a genuine advance. It needed 3.4 GB and 180 milliseconds per frame. On the MK-4 it could not be loaded at all.

In June, Devyani presented the Vision line at a Mumbai industry conference. The deck credited “the Madhukosh engineering team”; the trade coverage credited Devyani. Shirish's absence from the stage became a fixed item in the Pune team's account of itself. Almost nobody knew that she had asked him to co-present in April and he had declined: his father's surgery was that week, and he did not want it discussed.

In July, at the quarterly business review, Devyani was asked why the November module was at risk. Manjhi Systems: The Friday Skip-Level

Bengaluru, Monday, 8 September 2026

1. Opening

At 7:40 a.m. Ananya Krishnan was already at her desk on the fourth floor of Manjhi Systems' office on Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road, reading a calendar invitation she had not sent. Rohit Dere, the engineering lead in Pune who ran the nine-person pod building the Tanweer Finance reconciliation module, had booked thirty minutes with Priya Raman, the VP of Engineering, for Friday at 4 p.m. The subject line read "Pune pod — workload and planning concerns." Ananya was not invited, and Rohit had not spoken to her about it first.

She had until Friday to decide what to do. The reconciliation module was due to go live for Tanweer Finance, a Dubai-based digital lender, on 25 September — seventeen days away — ahead of a UAE Central Bank Open Finance certification deadline that Tanweer could not miss without losing its provisional licence extension. Whatever Rohit said in that meeting, and whatever Ananya did before it, would decide both the shape of the launch and whether she kept the trust of the team she needed to deliver it.

2. Company background

Manjhi Systems, founded in Bengaluru in 2016, builds reconciliation and compliance-automation software for non-banking financial companies, digital lenders and small finance banks. Its product ingests settlement files from UPI and NPCI rails, pulls consented data through India's Account Aggregator framework, and reconciles a lender's ledger against its banking partners' records — work that used to take finance teams days and now runs overnight. Manjhi handles personal financial data under the DPDP Act and is audited annually by its larger clients' compliance teams as a condition of the contract.

The company has 214 client accounts and roughly ₹58 crore in annual recurring revenue, with 190 employees split between a go-to-market and product team in Bengaluru and a 55-engineer delivery organisation in Pune. It competes for enterprise accounts against Perfios, M2P Fintech and Signzy, and increasingly against in-house teams at larger NBFCs; its edge has been faster integration and a reconciliation engine that clients say needs less manual override than rivals'. In 2025 it began selling into the Gulf, where DIFC-regulated lenders were adopting frameworks similar to India's — Tanweer Finance, signed in March 2026, was its second Middle East account and by far its largest, at ₹14.6 crore a year.

3. The situation

Ananya, 34, joined Manjhi as a product manager two years ago after four years as a backend engineer at a payments company. She owns the Tanweer workstream end to end: requirements, specification and the relationship with Mei-Ling Tan, the Singapore-based customer success lead who manages the account. Rohit's pod builds it.

Over the six weeks before this Monday, the working relationship had degraded in ways Ananya had not fully registered until the calendar invite. In late July she went quiet on the roadmap for nearly three weeks while she sat with Tanweer's compliance team in a series of video calls to pin down exact reconciliation rules for Islamic financing products — work she felt she could not delegate because it was still forming. Rohit's engineers, mid-sprint on the assumption that scope was fixed, had no visibility into what was changing and stopped attending her stand-ins. On 18 August, at the quarterly business review, a director asked why the reconciliation SLA had slipped for two client accounts; Ananya, without checking first, told the room it was an engineering execution issue — when in fact she had changed the matching-rule specification mid-sprint twice that month. On 25 August she demoed the new rules engine to the regional leadership team alone, presenting it as work she had "pushed through," without Rohit or any engineer in the room, though three of them had rebuilt the core matcher in nine days. On 3 September she sent the pod a 46-page specification for the remaining Tanweer scope — exact field mappings, exact retry logic, exact error codes — with a ten-day deadline and no design conversation beforehand.

From Pune, Rohit saw a pattern, not four incidents. From Berlin, Lukas Brandt, the lead product designer, had separately noticed that onboarding-flow decisions were being made and announced rather than reviewed with him. From Singapore, Mei-Ling saw only that the date was closer and Tanweer's compliance officer was asking sharper questions each week. From New Jersey, Derek Walsh, the sales head for strategic accounts, saw a ₹14.6 crore renewal at risk if the date slipped. Nobody but Rohit had connected the sprint data to the relationship — until he booked the skip-level.

Ask Mei-Ling to test whether Tanweer will accept a phased go-live: core reconciliation live 25 September as promised, edge-case handling for Islamic financing products by 5 October, which matches what Sprint 24's delivered-to-planned ratio (44 of 68 points, 65%) suggests is realistic anyway. 7. Questions for discussion

  1. Match each of Ananya's actions between 21 July and 3 September to one of the five behaviours this topic names — being mysterious, explaining how instead of what, hoarding credit, throwing blame, and hurry-up-then-wait. Which single incident, if reversed, would have changed the most?

  3. Rohit, Lukas, Mei-Ling and Derek each see a different part of this problem from a different city. What would each of them need to hear from Ananya before Friday for a decision to hold across all four?

8. A note for the learner

This topic is useful here because it turns a vague complaint — "the PM is hard to work with" — into five specific, checkable behaviours, each visible in the case: going quiet on the roadmap for three weeks (mysterious), writing a 46-page specification instead of a problem statement (explaining how), presenting the rules engine alone (hoarding credit), telling the QBR the SLA slip was an execution issue (throwing blame), and compressing three weeks of silence into a ten-day deadline (hurry-up-then-wait). A well-reasoned answer does not treat Friday's meeting as a scheduling problem to smooth over; it treats it as the moment those five behaviours either get named and corrected, or get confirmed by how Ananya handles the next eleven days.

Option A fixes nothing the pod is reacting to and risks confirming, through a bonus rather than a change in behaviour, that the pattern will continue. Option C removes Ananya from the friction without addressing the habits that caused it, and trades a short-term fix for a longer-term credibility cost. Option B is the defensible path: it corrects the record on the QBR, converts a solution-dictating specification into a problem statement the engineers can own, shares credit for work already done, and — critically — adjusts scope through a phased launch rather than asking the team to absorb both a compressed deadline and a trust repair in the same eleven days. It costs Ananya an uncomfortable conversation and asks Mei-Ling to manage the client relationship more actively, but it is the only option that treats the sprint-data decline in Exhibit 1 as connected to the incidents in Exhibit 2, rather than as two separate problems. The programmes that teach this module well warn against solving it with more agile ceremony — another retro, another stand-up ritual. The fix here is not process; it is Ananya changing five specific things she does, starting before Friday, not after it.

How Product Managers Alienate Engineers

Five ordinary behaviours — being mysterious, explaining how, hoarding credit, throwing blame, and hurrying up then waiting — and why the damage shows up as silence rather than complaint.

1. Bengaluru, 3 March 2026: a number Meera did not expect

Meera Rajagopal had been a senior product manager at Chaturanga Systems for fourteen months. Chaturanga sells warehouse and replenishment software to mid-market Indian retailers — 410 customers, ₹86 crore of annual recurring revenue, 240 employees in a converted textile building off Hosur Road. Meera owned Inventory & Replenishment, the area that decides how much stock each store should hold and when it should be topped up. It was the part of the product customers renewed for.

On the morning of 3 March, Deepa Iyer, the engineering manager she worked with, sent her the quarterly engineering pulse results filtered to Meera's two squads. One line item read: “My product manager helps me understand why we are building this.” Fourteen months earlier it had scored 4.3 out of 5. It now read 2.9. A second line, tracked by Deepa privately, was worse: the share of risks that engineers raised before they became incidents had fallen from 71 per cent to 22 per cent. Karthik Nambiar, a backend engineer with four years of context on the stock-ledger service, had resigned on 20 February. Two others had, Deepa said carefully, “been taking calls.”

The stakes were specific. The replenishment forecasting rewrite was due on 30 June for a 210-store grocery chain headquartered in Coimbatore whose renewal, worth ₹4.2 crore, depended on it. That rewrite needed exactly the people who were quietly leaving, and it needed them to volunteer bad news early. Meera's instinct was that the number measured the workload, not her. The data said otherwise: the neighbouring squad, running the same release cadence under a different PM, had scored 4.1.

2. The idea: alienation is a withdrawal, not an argument

Alienation, in this context, means the progressive withdrawal of two things an engineer gives voluntarily and cannot be compelled to give: discretionary effort (the care taken beyond what a ticket literally requires) and discretionary disclosure (saying out loud that something looks wrong before anyone has asked). Neither appears in a job description. Both are the difference between a team that ships and a team that merely closes tickets.

The vocabulary is old. Karl Marx used alienated labour in his 1844 manuscripts to name the condition of a worker separated from the purpose and the product of their work. The modern managerial version arrives through Frederick Herzberg's motivation-hygiene research in 1959, which found that the factors that make work satisfying are not the ones whose absence makes it miserable, and through Edward Deci and Richard Ryan's self-determination theory, formalised in 1985, which holds that sustained intrinsic motivation rests on three needs: autonomy (control over how one works), competence (visible mastery), and relatedness (belonging to a purpose shared with others). Tom DeMarco and Timothy Lister brought this into software with Peopleware in 1987; Kent Beck made it procedural in Extreme Programming in 1999, with the rule that the customer decides what and the developers decide how; and Teresa Amabile's 2011 work on the progress principle showed that the single largest daily driver of good “inner work life” is visible progress on meaningful work — which a PM can destroy simply by making the meaning invisible.

The sentence Meera could say in a room without sounding glib is this: “I own the why and the when-it-matters; you own the how; and I will name you in the room where credit is handed out.” Everything that follows is an elaboration of where those three clauses get broken.

3. How it actually works: trust is a stock, not a flow

The mechanics are easiest to see if trust is treated as a stock — a quantity held in a tank, drained by events and refilled by a slow inflow — rather than as a mood. Three properties of the stock do all the explanatory work, and practitioners routinely leave all three implicit.

First, the drain is far wider than the inflow. A single public reassignment of blame in a Monday business review can remove what four weeks of reliable behaviour deposited. In Deepa's own tracking at Chaturanga, an engineer who had experienced one blame event took a median of seven weeks before their pre-emptive disclosure rate returned to baseline, against a single Monday for the event itself. This is not sentimentality; it is Bayesian. One observation of a PM behaving badly under pressure is highly informative about behaviour under pressure, because pressure is rare. Twenty observations of a PM behaving well when nothing is at stake are nearly uninformative.

Second, context decays. Meera told her squads in November why the forecasting rewrite mattered. By February, three of the seven engineers had joined after that conversation, the customer's renewal terms had changed, and the two engineers who had been in the room had each absorbed a different version. Context is not delivered; it is maintained. The implicit step almost every PM skips is re-supply: repeating the why at the start of each cycle, including the parts that have changed and the parts that have not.

Third, the stock is held by individuals, not by teams. When Karthik resigned, his trust balance left with him; the balance Meera had with Farhan Qureshi, the staff engineer with nine years of tenure, was untouched by that event but was doing a great deal of quiet work holding the squad together. A PM who reads a team-average score will systematically miss the two people whose departure would actually hurt.

4. A worked example: the code-red sprint that cost ₹18 lakh

On 2 February 2026 Meera walked into the squad's planning session and said that the multi-location replenishment override had to be done by the end of the sprint because “the Coimbatore account is at risk.” That was true in the loose sense that every large renewal is at risk. What she did not say, because she did not think it mattered, was that the commercial decision on that renewal was not scheduled until 24 March. The squad rearranged everything.

At ₹24,000 per loaded engineer-day that is ₹4.08 lakh, and the service credits add ₹14.0 lakh, for ₹18.08 lakh of cost. The only input that changed was a sentence containing a date, and it was worth ₹18.08 lakh.

There is a second, slower arithmetic that matters more. Deepa's squads surface roughly 18 material risks a quarter. At 71 per cent pre-emptive disclosure, 12.8 of those are caught early and 5.2 late. At 22 per cent, 4.0 are early and 14.0 late. Chaturanga's own post-incident reviews put the average extra cost of a late-caught risk at 3.2 engineer-days. So the disclosure collapse costs (14.0 − 5.2) × 3.2 = 28.2 engineer-days per quarter, about ₹6.8 lakh, every quarter, invisibly, with no incident to point at.

5. Nuances a learner must get straight

Alienation is not disagreement

A squad that argues with its PM about scope is not alienated; it is engaged. Argument costs energy, and engineers spend energy on things they expect to influence. The signal of alienation is the disappearance of argument — the meeting where the estimate is accepted without a fight and the ticket is closed exactly as written. Meera's first mistake was reading the quiet January planning sessions as alignment.

“Explain how” is about mechanism, not about specificity

PMs are sometimes told the lesson is “be less prescriptive,” which they hear as “be vaguer,” and vagueness alienates faster than over-specification. The real line is between outcome and mechanism. “Replenishment suggestions must appear within 400 milliseconds at the 95th percentile, for a store with 12,000 SKUs” is an outcome, however precise. “Cache the suggestions in Redis” is a mechanism, and it belongs to the engineers unless they have invited the PM into it.

Confidentiality is real; unexplained silence is not the same as a secret

Sometimes a PM genuinely cannot say why priorities changed — an acquisition, a legal matter, an unannounced customer. Being mysterious is not the same as being discreet. The discreet move is to name the shape of the secret: “There is a commercial reason I can't describe until the 14th; it is not about your work, and I will tell you the whole thing on the 15th.” That sentence costs nothing and preserves the stock.

Credit hoarding is usually structural, not moral

Meera did not intend to take credit. She wrote the launch note, so her name sat at the top of it; she presented at the business review, so the questions came to her; she was the one the VP thanked. Nobody in the chain did anything greedy, and the engineers still watched a quarter of their work get narrated by someone else. Because the cause is structural, the fix is structural: attribution has to be written down somewhere durable, by name, in the artefact that leadership actually reads.

Blame is nearly always thrown at a third party, and lands anyway

Almost no PM says “Farhan was late.” What they say, to a stakeholder, is “engineering slipped.” It feels impersonal. It is not: the squad reads the update, and the passive construction is understood as a refusal to share ownership of a date that the PM also agreed to. The available alternative is not self-flagellation but the first-person plural — “we found a data-migration problem we had not priced, and here is the new date and why we believe it.”

Hurry-up-then-wait is the most expensive of the five

The other four damage a relationship. This one damages an instrument. After two false alarms, a PM's urgency signal carries no information, which means that on the day something genuinely is on fire, the squad's response is indistinguishable from its response to a normal Tuesday. The cost is not paid at the time of the false alarm; it is paid later, once, at the worst possible moment.

What the idea cannot tell you

Nothing in this topic can distinguish an alienated team from a team that is simply not good enough. Both look like slow delivery, low disclosure and defensive estimates. A PM who has just read about alienation will over-diagnose it, and a PM who has just been through a bad quarter will under-diagnose it. The only reliable separator is the counterfactual: does the same team disclose freely to someone else? Deepa's comparison with the neighbouring squad — same cadence, same codebase, different PM, 4.1 versus 2.9 — was that counterfactual.

The deficit may not be yours

Trust balances are inherited. An engineer who was burned by the previous PM will test a new one for months, and the new PM will experience this as unfair. It is unfair, and it is also rational on the engineer's part. The only response that works is time plus an unbroken record, which is why the questions a thoughtful newcomer should ask on joining an area are: What did the last PM promise that did not happen? Who here has been overruled on a technical decision, and by whom? When was the last time someone raised a risk early and was rewarded for it?

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

The five behaviours are universal, but their relative danger is not. The differences that are real are set out below; where a difference is often claimed but does not hold, it is worth saying so plainly. The idea that engineers in consumer companies care more about purpose than engineers in enterprise companies, for example, does not survive contact with evidence — enterprise engineers care about purpose just as much, they simply have to be told the purpose because they will never meet the user by accident.

At 900, she could not, and the repair would have to run through managers and written artefacts rather than through her presence, which is slower and less convincing.

7. Common mistakes, and the cheapest test that catches each

Each of the mistakes below is ordinary, well-intentioned, and visible from outside if you know what to look at. The diagnostics are deliberately cheap: none takes more than a few minutes, because a diagnostic that requires a survey cycle will not be run.

8. What good looks like

Consider the same February request handled by Anand Sethuraman, the PM on the neighbouring squad, when his own escalation arrived on 5 February. He spent forty minutes before the planning meeting establishing three facts: who would decide, what they would decide, and on what date. He then opened planning with the constraint rather than the emotion — the decision was on 19 March, the demo had to exist by 12 March, and everything else was negotiable. He offered a sequencing he thought made sense and said explicitly that the sequencing was a suggestion, not a specification. When the squad proposed a narrower first cut that met the demo requirement with 60 per cent of the work, he took it without counter-argument, which is the single most trust-generative act available to a PM.

Three weeks later, the demo slipped by four days because of an authentication problem nobody had foreseen. Anand's stakeholder note said: “We mis-scoped the tenant authentication work; Sneha Balakrishnan found it on the 8th, which is why we are four days late rather than three weeks late.” That sentence did two jobs at once — it shared the ownership of the miss and it rewarded the early disclosure by name. The neighbouring squad's pre-emptive disclosure rate that quarter was 74 per cent.

9. What Meera decided

Meera's instinct on 3 March was to call a team meeting and apologise. Deepa talked her out of it, on the grounds that a group apology asks the injured party to do emotional work in public and produces exactly the polite silence that caused the misreading in the first place. What Meera did instead had three parts, and the reasoning behind each is the argument of this page in miniature.

She wrote a one-page “why” document for the forecasting rewrite, dated and versioned, and committed to re-reading it aloud at the start of every cycle — because context decays and must be re-supplied. She rewrote her stakeholder update template so that every slip sentence began with “we” and every shipped item carried the names of the engineers who built it — because blame and credit are structural, and structures are what you can actually change. And she made a rule for herself that she would not use the word “urgent” without attaching a decision date and a decider's name, which meant that for six weeks she used it once — because an urgency signal is only worth what its base rate makes it worth. She did not expect the pulse score to move for two quarters, and told Deepa so.

What to learn next follows directly. The natural successor topic is the PM–engineering working agreement: the short, explicit, written contract that converts all of the above from good intentions into commitments a squad can hold a PM to. It is the mechanism by which the argument here stops depending on the PM's memory. Behind it sits the wider study of the PM–engineering relationship, of which alienation is simply the failure case.

Two questions to sit with. First: in your current team, when did someone last tell you something you did not want to hear, unprompted — and what happened to them afterwards? Second: if you wrote down every time in the last quarter you used urgency as a persuasion device, how many of those outputs were used on the date you implied?
